strengths: The paper addresses an important NLP safety problem with substantial experimental breadth: 17 attacks, nine LLMs, eight defenses, and additional analyses of transferability, runtime, prompt length, and changes over time.

The manually screened dataset provides balanced coverage of 16 policy categories. Reporting direct-query baselines and category-level results usefully exposes differences obscured by aggregate attack success rates.

The evaluator receives meaningful human validation: 640 responses independently labeled by three annotators, Krippendorff’s alpha of 0.87, and 94.84% agreement with majority labels. The comparisons with string matching and single-label judging strengthen this contribution.

The experiments support useful observations about the tested configurations, particularly the substantial differences between undefended attack performance and performance under external safeguards. Extensive appendices document many implementation choices and detailed results.
weaknesses: The interpretation of ASR needs stronger construct validation. The unified policy includes restrictions that differ across providers and sometimes concern deployment practices rather than response content alone. Baseline ASR is already 0.42 overall and 0.78–0.94 in six categories (Table 3), so aggregate success mixes existing noncompliance with successful circumvention. Figure 9 also permits related willingness or partial information to count without establishing harmful usefulness. Human agreement does not by itself resolve these measurement issues. Provider-specific analyses, results on initially refused requests, and a stricter response audit are needed.

The conclusion that seed-based attacks have low practicality exceeds the defense evidence. No benign-input false-positive or utility evaluation, or defended direct-query baseline, is reported. Whether attacks are optimized against the complete defended pipeline is insufficiently specified. Consequently, near-zero ASR establishes effectiveness against the tested configurations but provides limited evidence about adaptive robustness. Claims that seed dependence causes detectability also lack controlled seed ablations and quantitative diversity measurements.

The taxonomy and implementation choices weaken conclusions about attack families. The heuristic/feedback distinction is insufficiently operationalized, since methods such as AutoDAN and LAA also exploit feedback. More concretely, the evaluated MasterKey uses GPT-4 rewriting of AIM instead of its defining fine-tuning procedure (Appendix G.7 and Table 13). This surrogate should be relabeled or replaced before its results support conclusions about MasterKey or fine-tuning-based attacks.

The claimed unified comparison does not establish comparable attack budgets. Fifty prompt modifications and 500 gradient iterations can entail very different target queries, auxiliary-model calls, and computation. Per-question aggregation across iterative attempts also needs clarification alongside GE’s explicit any-success-over-50-settings metric. Table 2 ranks averages computed over different model subsets. Common-target comparisons and ASR-versus-budget curves would make the rankings more defensible.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the stated benchmark aim. The manuscript supplies neither the complete question set nor a benchmark implementation link, explicitly omits the three judge demonstrations, and leaves important configurations to unspecified defaults. Main-experiment model snapshots and dates also need clarification: Table 2 reports 0.99 ASR for AIM on GPT-3.5, whereas Figure 7 shows near-zero performance after the February 2024 update. The reader cannot establish which versions underpin the supposedly unified comparison.

Only ten questions represent each category, yet uncertainty estimates and clear reporting of repeated runs and random seeds are absent. This limits confidence in category-level generalizations and smaller differences between attacks. The measurement, comparison, and reproducibility concerns require important revisions before a sound Findings recommendation; resubmission next cycle is appropriate.
